## Introduction

This report analyzes the TidyTuesday dataset from Adam Kucharski's online quiz "How likely is 'likely'?", in which more than 5,000 participants assigned numeric probabilities (0–100%) to 19 everyday probability phrases and compared pairs of those phrases. The quiz also collected respondent demographics such as age band, English-language background, education level, and country of residence. The released data include absolute probability judgements, pairwise comparison choices, and respondent metadata. Here I focus on two questions: (1) which phrases people disagree on most when translating them into numeric probabilities, and (2) which demographic backgrounds tend to assign higher probabilities—i.e., appear more "optimistic"—after controlling for phrase.

## Setup and Data Loading

The following chunk imports the packages used throughout the report.

## Data Checks

The TidyTuesday curators note that no cleaning was necessary. The checks below verify that claim for the absolute judgements and pairwise tables, and document missingness in the demographic metadata.

```{python}
#| label: data-checks
#| warning: false

# (a) Missing values per column
print("(a) Missing values per column")
print("absolute_judgements:\n", judgements.isna().sum().to_string(), "\n")
print("pairwise_comparisons:\n", pairwise.isna().sum().to_string(), "\n")
print("respondent_metadata:\n", metadata.isna().sum().to_string(), "\n")

# (b) Probability range
prob_min = judgements["probability"].min()
prob_max = judgements["probability"].max()
n_out_of_range = ((judgements["probability"] < 0) | (judgements["probability"] > 100)).sum()
print(f"(b) Probability min={prob_min}, max={prob_max}; outside 0-100: {n_out_of_range}")

# (c) Unique terms
terms = sorted(judgements["term"].unique())
print(f"(c) Unique terms: {len(terms)}")
print(terms)

# (d) Unique respondents and set differences
j_ids = set(judgements["response_id"].unique())
p_ids = set(pairwise["response_id"].unique())
m_ids = set(metadata["response_id"].unique())
print(
    f"(d) Unique respondents — judgements: {len(j_ids)}, "
    f"pairwise: {len(p_ids)}, metadata: {len(m_ids)}"
)
print(f"    In judgements but not metadata: {len(j_ids - m_ids)}")
print(f"    In metadata but not judgements: {len(m_ids - j_ids)}")
print(f"    In pairwise but not metadata: {len(p_ids - m_ids)}")

# (e) Terms per respondent
terms_per = judgements.groupby("response_id")["term"].nunique()
print("(e) Terms per respondent value counts:")
print(terms_per.value_counts().sort_index().to_string())
print(f"    Respondents with != 19 terms: {(terms_per != 19).sum()}")

# (f) Duplicate (response_id, term) rows
n_dup_pairs = judgements.duplicated(subset=["response_id", "term"]).sum()
print(f"(f) Duplicate (response_id, term) rows: {n_dup_pairs}")

# (g) Demographic unique values
print("(g) Demographic unique values")
print("age_band:", sorted(metadata["age_band"].dropna().unique().tolist()))
print(
    "english_background:",
    sorted(metadata["english_background"].dropna().unique().tolist()),
)
print(
    "education_level:",
    sorted(metadata["education_level"].dropna().unique().tolist()),
)
print(f"Unique countries: {metadata['country_of_residence'].nunique(dropna=True)}")
```

**What the checks found.** Absolute judgements and pairwise comparisons have no missing values. All probability ratings fall within 0–100. There are exactly 19 unique terms, and every one of the 5,174 respondents appears in all three tables with no mismatches. Every respondent rated all 19 terms exactly once (no duplicate `(response_id, term)` rows). Demographic fields do have missing values: age band (437), English background (421), education level (663), and country of residence (720), with 64 unique countries among non-missing responses.

**Decisions.** No rows are dropped from the judgement or pairwise tables. For demographic analyses later, respondents with missing values on a given demographic variable are excluded from that variable's grouping only (pairwise-complete cases). No imputation is applied.

## Question 1: Which phrases do people most disagree on, in relation to the probability they represent?

Using only `absolute_judgements`, I summarize how widely respondents disagree on the numeric probability attached to each phrase. **Disagreement** is defined as the standard deviation of assigned probabilities; the interquartile range (IQR) is used as a robustness check.

```{python}
#| label: q1-term-summary
#| warning: false

grouped = judgements.groupby("term")["probability"]
term_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "n": grouped.count(),
        "mean": grouped.mean(),
        "median": grouped.median(),
        "std": grouped.std(),
        "iqr": grouped.quantile(0.75) - grouped.quantile(0.25),
        "p10": grouped.quantile(0.10),
        "p90": grouped.quantile(0.90),
    }
)
term_summary["p10_p90_range"] = term_summary["p90"] - term_summary["p10"]
term_summary = term_summary.sort_values("std", ascending=False).round(2)
term_summary.index.name = "term"
display(term_summary.reset_index())

rank_sd = term_summary["std"].rank(ascending=False)
rank_iqr = term_summary["iqr"].rank(ascending=False)
rank_compare = pd.DataFrame({"rank_by_std": rank_sd, "rank_by_iqr": rank_iqr})
print("Top 5 by SD:", term_summary.head(5).index.tolist())
print("Top 5 by IQR:", term_summary.sort_values("iqr", ascending=False).head(5).index.tolist())
display(rank_compare.sort_values("rank_by_std").head(10))
```

The table is sorted by standard deviation (descending). The top four phrases by SD — *Realistic Possibility*, *Could Happen*, *Might Happen*, and *May Happen* — are also the top four by IQR, so those rankings agree closely. Lower in the list, rankings diverge somewhat (for example *Highly Unlikely* ranks high on SD but much lower on IQR because of a long right tail), so IQR is a useful robustness check for outlier-driven disagreement.

The box plot below shows the full distribution of assigned probabilities for each phrase, ordered by median probability so that the typical ranking of phrases is easy to read.

```{python}
#| label: q1-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "Horizontal box plots of assigned probability (%) by phrase, ordered by median probability."
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8

term_order_median = (
    judgements.groupby("term")["probability"].median().sort_values().index.tolist()
)
plot_df = judgements.copy()
plot_df["term"] = pd.Categorical(plot_df["term"], categories=term_order_median, ordered=True)

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))
sns.boxplot(
    data=plot_df,
    y="term",
    x="probability",
    color="#4C78A8",
    fliersize=1.5,
    linewidth=0.8,
    ax=ax,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Probability assigned (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Probability phrase")
ax.set_title("Distribution of assigned probabilities by phrase")
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Extreme certainty phrases (*Almost No Chance*, *Almost Certain*, *Will Happen*, *About Even*) have tight boxes near the edges or at 50%, while mid-probability phrases such as *Could Happen*, *Might Happen*, *May Happen*, and *Realistic Possibility* show much wider spreads.

The bar chart below ranks phrases by disagreement (standard deviation), with the most disputed phrases at the top.

```{python}
#| label: q1-disagreement-bars
#| fig-cap: "Standard deviation of assigned probability (%) by phrase, sorted descending so the most disputed phrases appear at the top."
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

sd_order = term_summary["std"].sort_values(ascending=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
ax.barh(sd_order.index, sd_order.values, color="#4C78A8")
ax.set_xlabel("Standard deviation of probability assigned (percentage points)")
ax.set_ylabel("Probability phrase")
ax.set_title("Disagreement by phrase (standard deviation)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

*Realistic Possibility* stands out with the largest standard deviation (~20.6 percentage points), followed by *Could Happen*, *Might Happen*, and *May Happen*. Phrases that imply near-certainty or near-impossibility, along with *About Even*, show the least disagreement.

**Answer to Question 1.** The most disputed phrases are *Realistic Possibility* (SD = 20.55, median = 60%), *Could Happen* (SD = 18.23, median = 40%), *Might Happen* (SD = 17.66, median = 40%), *May Happen* (SD = 17.02, median = 40%), and *Highly Unlikely* (SD = 12.41, median = 5%). Disagreement is highest for mid-range, hedged phrases whose typical ratings sit between roughly 40% and 60%, not for extreme phrases. Extreme phrases such as *About Even* (SD = 3.66), *Almost Certain* (SD = 5.79), and *Almost No Chance* (SD = 6.04) show much tighter agreement. The IQR ranking matches the SD ranking for the top mid-range phrases, which supports treating those phrases as the main locus of disagreement rather than an artifact of a few outliers.

## Question 2: Which demographic background is the most optimistic?

**Definition of "optimistic".** Here, a more optimistic respondent is one who assigns *higher probabilities to the same phrases on average*. That is a narrow, operational definition: it captures a tendency toward higher numeric ratings, not broader psychological optimism, risk appetite, or beliefs about future events. Limits of this definition include that (1) all phrases are rated in isolation from real-world stakes, (2) higher ratings on low-probability phrases and high-probability phrases are treated the same after centering, and (3) demographic differences may reflect language interpretation rather than outlook.

To control for term, I subtract each term's overall mean probability from each judgement, then average those deviations within respondent. I also compute each respondent's raw mean probability for comparison.

```{python}
#| label: q2-respondent-deviations
#| warning: false

# Term-level means and per-judgement deviations
term_mean_map = judgements.groupby("term")["probability"].mean()
judgements = judgements.copy()
judgements["term_mean"] = judgements["term"].map(term_mean_map)
judgements["deviation"] = judgements["probability"] - judgements["term_mean"]

# Respondent-level optimism scores
respondent_optimism = (
    judgements.groupby("response_id")
    .agg(
        mean_deviation=("deviation", "mean"),
        raw_mean_probability=("probability", "mean"),
        n_terms=("term", "count"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)

# Merge demographics
respondent_optimism = respondent_optimism.merge(metadata, on="response_id", how="left")

print(respondent_optimism[["mean_deviation", "raw_mean_probability"]].describe().round(3))
print(
    "Correlation between raw mean and mean deviation:",
    round(
        respondent_optimism["mean_deviation"].corr(
            respondent_optimism["raw_mean_probability"]
        ),
        4,
    ),
)
display(respondent_optimism.head())
```

Because every respondent rated the same 19 terms, mean deviation equals the raw mean probability minus a constant (the average of the 19 term means). The two scores are therefore perfectly correlated here; the deviation form still makes the “relative to the phrase mean” interpretation explicit for later group comparisons.

Group comparisons use a minimum of **30 respondents** per group. Groups below that threshold are excluded from ranking. Confidence intervals are **t-based 95% CIs** for the mean deviation. Kruskal–Wallis tests summarize overall differences; effect sizes (approximate η²) are emphasized over p-values. For country, only the top 15 countries by respondent count among those meeting the n ≥ 30 rule are shown (here, 12 countries qualify).

```{python}
#| label: q2-group-tables
#| warning: false

MIN_N = 30


def group_comparison(df, col, label, top_n=None):
    """Mean deviation by group with t-based 95% CI; keep groups with n >= MIN_N."""
    sub = df.dropna(subset=[col, "mean_deviation"]).copy()
    rows = []
    for name, s in sub.groupby(col)["mean_deviation"]:
        n = int(s.shape[0])
        mean = float(s.mean())
        if n > 1:
            se = float(s.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n))
            tcrit = float(stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n - 1))
            ci_low, ci_high = mean - tcrit * se, mean + tcrit * se
        else:
            ci_low = ci_high = np.nan
        rows.append(
            {
                "group": name,
                "n": n,
                "mean_deviation": mean,
                "ci_low": ci_low,
                "ci_high": ci_high,
            }
        )
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    n_total_groups = out.shape[0]
    out_qual = out[out["n"] >= MIN_N].copy()
    n_excluded = n_total_groups - out_qual.shape[0]

    if top_n is not None:
        counts = sub.groupby(col).size().sort_values(ascending=False)
        qualifying_counts = counts[counts >= MIN_N]
        top_groups = qualifying_counts.head(top_n).index
        out_qual = out_qual[out_qual["group"].isin(top_groups)]

    out_qual = out_qual.sort_values("mean_deviation", ascending=False).reset_index(
        drop=True
    )
    out_qual[["mean_deviation", "ci_low", "ci_high"]] = out_qual[
        ["mean_deviation", "ci_low", "ci_high"]
    ].round(3)

    # Kruskal-Wallis on all n >= MIN_N groups for this variable
    keep = sub.groupby(col).filter(lambda g: len(g) >= MIN_N)
    samples = [g["mean_deviation"].values for _, g in keep.groupby(col)]
    if len(samples) >= 2:
        H, p = stats.kruskal(*samples)
        k = len(samples)
        n = sum(len(s) for s in samples)
        eta2 = (H - k + 1) / (n - k) if (n - k) > 0 else np.nan
    else:
        H = p = eta2 = np.nan
        k = n = 0

    print(f"=== {label} ({col}) ===")
    print(
        f"Groups with n >= {MIN_N}: {out_qual.shape[0]} shown; "
        f"excluded below threshold: {n_excluded}"
        + (f"; capped at top {top_n} by count" if top_n else "")
    )
    display(out_qual)
    print(
        f"Kruskal-Wallis H={H:.2f}, p={p:.3g}, approx eta^2={eta2:.4f} "
        f"(k={k} groups, n={n} respondents)"
    )
    spread = out_qual["mean_deviation"].max() - out_qual["mean_deviation"].min()
    print(f"Spread (max − min mean deviation): {spread:.3f} percentage points\n")
    return out_qual


age_tbl = group_comparison(respondent_optimism, "age_band", "Age band")
eng_tbl = group_comparison(
    respondent_optimism, "english_background", "English background"
)
edu_tbl = group_comparison(respondent_optimism, "education_level", "Education level")
country_tbl = group_comparison(
    respondent_optimism,
    "country_of_residence",
    "Country of residence",
    top_n=15,
)

# Store for plotting
q2_tables = {
    "Age band": age_tbl,
    "English background": eng_tbl,
    "Education level": edu_tbl,
    "Country of residence": country_tbl,
}
```

Excluded groups with n < 30 were *Under 18* (age) and *Less than high school* (education). For country, 12 countries met the sample-size threshold (so the “top 15 qualifying” list is those 12). Education shows the largest spread among the multi-category demographics in the tables above; English-background differences are near zero.

The forest-style plots below show each group's mean deviation with its 95% t-based CI. Groups are ordered by mean deviation; the dashed line at 0 is the overall phrase-adjusted average.

```{python}
#| label: q2-forest-plots
#| fig-cap: "Mean phrase-adjusted probability deviation (percentage points) by demographic group, with 95% t-based confidence intervals. Positive values indicate higher-than-average probability assignments (more 'optimistic' under the operational definition)."
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))
panel_order = [
    ("Age band", age_tbl),
    ("English background", eng_tbl),
    ("Education level", edu_tbl),
    ("Country of residence", country_tbl),
]

for ax, (title, tbl) in zip(axes.flat, panel_order):
    # Order ascending so highest optimism appears at top of horizontal plot
    plot_tbl = tbl.sort_values("mean_deviation", ascending=True).reset_index(drop=True)
    y = np.arange(len(plot_tbl))
    x = plot_tbl["mean_deviation"].values
    xerr = np.vstack(
        [
            x - plot_tbl["ci_low"].values,
            plot_tbl["ci_high"].values - x,
        ]
    )
    ax.errorbar(
        x,
        y,
        xerr=xerr,
        fmt="o",
        color="#4C78A8",
        ecolor="#4C78A8",
        elinewidth=1.2,
        capsize=3,
        markersize=5,
    )
    ax.axvline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax.set_yticks(y)
    # Shorten long English labels for readability
    labels = [
        (
            g.replace("English is not my first language and I am not fluent", "Non-fluent L2")
            .replace("English is not my first language but I am fluent", "Fluent L2")
            .replace("English is my first language", "L1 English")
        )
        for g in plot_tbl["group"]
    ]
    ax.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("Mean deviation (percentage points)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.grid(axis="x", linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)

fig.suptitle("Optimism by demographic group (phrase-adjusted)", fontsize=13, y=1.01)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Across panels, education and country show clearer separations than English background. High school and some-college groups sit above zero, while postgraduate sits slightly below; among countries with enough respondents, the United States is above zero and Norway is below.
